chief_complaint: constant left lower quadrant abdominal pain and fever
hpi_details: A 35-year-old male presents to the clinic with constant left lower quadrant abdominal pain and fever. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: He thinks he caught a severe stomach bug or food poisoning from some suspect leftovers he ate.
concerns: He is worried that his appendix has burst and that emergency surgery will cause him to miss an essential project deadline at work.
expectations: He hopes to be prescribed strong antibiotics and painkillers so he can recover at home without being admitted.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Acute Diverticulitis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management for Acute Diverticulitis emphasizes a clear liquid diet with oral Ciprofloxacin and Metronidazole, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Acute Diverticulitis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Colorectal cancer without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Diffuse peritonitis.

boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

must_ask.say: How long has this been going on?
Any change in your bowel habits?

history.answer: My lower left belly has been hurting constantly, and I've been running a fever.
The pain started about three days ago as a dull discomfort, but it gradually became sharper and constant.
It has stayed right here in my lower left abdomen the entire time; it hasn't shifted anywhere else.
No, the pain doesn't shoot into my back, groin, or shoulder.
It is a steady, constant aching throb that doesn't come and go in waves.
It began at around a 4 out of 10, but over the last two days it has worsened to about a 7 out of 10.
Moving around or walking makes the throbbing worse, and eating seems to upset it. Staying still in bed gives me the most relief.
No, I've had mild constipation before, but never severe or constant pain like this.
I've felt mildly nauseated and lost my appetite, but I haven't thrown up at all.
I've been feeling constipated for the past two days and having trouble passing gas, but there has been no diarrhea or blood in my stool.
Yes, I measured my temperature yesterday and it was around 38.0 degrees, and I've had mild chills.
No, my eyes and skin haven't turned yellow, and my urine and stool colors look normal.
I don't have any pain or burning when I urinate, no frequent urge to pee, and no blood in my urine.
No, I haven't felt lightheaded, dizzy, or like I was going to faint.
No, I don't have any chest tightness, shortness of breath, or cough.
history.topic: Chest pain and shortness of breath

history.answer: I haven't eaten any unusually greasy foods, and I haven't had any alcohol over the past few days.
I took two acetaminophen tablets yesterday to bring down the fever, but I haven't taken any ibuprofen or aspirin.
No, I have never had any irregular heartbeats, blood clots, or circulation problems.
I have been feeling completely drained and worn out since the pain and fever started.
I was wondering if I just picked up a really bad stomach bug or food poisoning from some old takeout I ate.
I'm really terrified that my appendix burst and I'll need emergency surgery right when I have a huge deadline at work.
I don't have any chronic illnesses like high blood pressure, diabetes, or bowel conditions.
I have never had surgery or stayed in a hospital before.
I don't take any regular prescription medications or vitamins, just the acetaminophen I took yesterday.
I have no known allergies to any medications, foods, or materials.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco products.
I only drink socially, maybe one or two beers on the weekend.
I work as an office manager and live in an apartment with my wife.
My father was diagnosed with diverticulitis in his fifties, but there is no family history of colon cancer or chronic bowel disease.

exam.finding: The patient appears tired and mildly uncomfortable, lying still on the examination bed.
Blood pressure 124/78 mmHg, heart rate 92 bpm, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, body temperature 38.1°C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Conjunctivae are pink without pallor; sclerae are clear without jaundice.
Abdomen is flat and symmetrical with no distension, rashes, or surgical scars.
Bowel sounds are hypoactive across all quadrants; no abdominal bruits heard.
Tympanitic note throughout; light percussion produces localized discomfort in the left lower quadrant.
Marked focal tenderness with mild voluntary guarding in the left lower quadrant; no palpable mass and other quadrants are soft and nontender.
Mild localized rebound tenderness in the left lower quadrant; no generalized abdominal rigidity.
Murphy sign is negative with no right upper quadrant tenderness or inspiratory arrest.
McBurney point, Rovsing, psoas, and obturator signs are all negative.
No costovertebral angle tenderness on either side.
No focal mass or tenderness appreciated on digital examination; no blood seen on the glove.
